theme: Where are you, LORD?, the lament when God seems hidden
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 10. After the prologue of Job, this is the psalm of someone who is living inside the silence. Read it slowly and listen for how the psalmist moves from accusation to confidence.
settingTheScene: Psalm 10 was probably written by David, and in many ancient manuscripts it was joined with Psalm 9 as a single poem. Psalm 9 celebrates God’s justice. Psalm 10 asks where that justice has gone. It is a lament about wicked people who seem to flourish while the poor are crushed. You have just watched Job lose everything while the wicked go on living. This psalm gives you words for what that feels like.
observation: The psalm opens with two questions: “Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?” (v. 1).
The wicked man hunts the poor and boasts about his desires (vv. 2-3).
He does not seek God, and “all his thoughts are, There is no God” (v. 4).
He believes he will never be moved, and he treats God as if God has forgotten (vv. 5-6, 11).
His mouth is full of lies and oppression, and he lies in wait like a lion (vv. 7-10).
In verse 12 the psalmist cries, “Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted.”
In verse 14 the psalmist says, “But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation.” The tone turns.
The psalm ends with confidence: “The LORD is king forever and ever” (v. 16), and he will “do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed” (v. 18).
interpretation:
The honesty of this psalm is part of its gift. It begins with a question that sounds close to an accusation: why do you hide? The Bible does not tell you to suppress that question. It hands you a prayer that asks it out loud. Prayer in the Psalms is not polite. It is true.

The middle of the psalm is a portrait of the wicked, and the details are chilling. The wicked man is proud, he is a predator, and he has talked himself into believing that nobody is watching. “God will never see it” (v. 11). Look at what drives his behavior. It is not that he has weighed the evidence and decided God does not exist. It is that he wants the freedom to do what he wants without anyone looking. Practical atheism works like that.

Then the turn at verse 12. The psalmist does not receive an answer to his question. What he does is change what he asks for. “Arise, O LORD” is a petition, and the petition quickly becomes a confession: “But you do see.” The same God who seemed to be hiding is now the God who notes every wrong. The psalmist has not changed his circumstances. He has recalled who God is.

The last verses are certain. “The LORD is king forever and ever.” The wicked have a short reign, and God has a permanent one. The psalm ends with the fatherless and the oppressed, because they are the ones God is listening to. “O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted” (v. 17).

This is how lament works. It states the problem honestly, it asks, and then it lets the character of God answer. Job will do exactly this over the next thirty-five chapters.
connection: The psalm describes the kind of arrogance that Paul quotes in Romans 3:14 (“Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness”), taken from verse 7. Jesus said that God will “give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night” (Luke 18:7). Revelation 6:10 hears the martyrs ask the same question, “How long, O Lord?”
application:
If God feels distant right now, pray this psalm back to him word for word. Do not clean up the question. Then, as the psalmist does, say out loud one thing you know to be true of God: that he sees, that he is king, that he hears the afflicted.

Also, take note of who in your life is being crushed by someone more powerful, and ask what a God who hears the afflicted would want you to do.
prayerPrompts: Tell God plainly where he seems far away.
Pray for someone who is afflicted and ask how you might help.
Ask him to strengthen your heart to wait.
